Following up on #41129 / #41131: I'd like to add the representer theorem (Kimeldorf–Wahba) to Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/Reproducing.lean.

Why it belongs here: it's the structural result that makes regularized estimation in an RKHS tractable — it guarantees that the minimizer of a regularized objective over the infinite-dimensional space H is a finite linear combination of the kernel sections kerFun H xᵢ at the data points, collapsing the problem to finite dimensions. It's the cornerstone of regularization theory in RKHS and the natural capstone of this file, and despite its applied reach it's a purely functional-analytic fact: orthogonal projection + the reproducing property.

Statement (scalar V = 𝕜 first; the precise "objective sees only the values on the data points" phrasing TBD):

theorem ... (s : Finset X) (Ω : ℝ → ℝ) (hΩ : StrictMono Ω) (L : (X → 𝕜) → ℝ) (f : H)
    (hf : IsMinOn (fun g : H => L g + Ω ‖g‖) Set.univ f) :
    f ∈ Submodule.span 𝕜 (Set.range fun i : s => kerFun H (i : X))

Proof: project f onto span{kerFun H xᵢ} (finite-dim ⇒ closed ⇒ projection exists); the reproducing property (inner_kerFun) fixes every f(xᵢ), so the data-fit term is unchanged, and Pythagoras + StrictMono Ω force the orthogonal part to vanish. Self-contained on current mathlib — no new imports.

I'm planning to start on it shortly; flagging mainly to coordinate — is anyone already on a representer theorem, and any preference on scalar (V = 𝕜) vs vector-valued first, or on naming? cc @Hampus Nyberg @Tjeerd Jan Heeringa @Yaël Dillies

Hello @Hao Zhang! As a moderator, I'd like to ask: have you seen mathlib's AI policy #use-of-ai? In particular, using an LLM to write comments on github or zulip is against the terms of this site. I'm asking because your post shares certain characteristics of LLM-generated writing.

1) If there is no draft, you can assume no one is close to finishing a PR on it.
2) In general, more general is more better. So, do vector-valued instead of scalar-valued.
3) For naming, I suggest you look into the documentation for it at https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/index.html or similar theorems in Loogle. You get something like mem_span_kerFun with a docstring explaining that its the representer theorem. However, be aware that Kimeldorf-Wahba is not the version you are sketching.
